--- title: "Quick Start" guide-section: "Getting Started" tags: [Tutorial, HTML] bread-crumbs: false --- This page walks you through the essentials of converting Markdown to HTML with multimark, covering inline formatting, block elements, smart punctuation, and safe HTML handling. ## Your First Conversion The most common task is converting Markdown to HTML. Import the renderer and pass it a string. ::: {#480ffe80 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from multimark import markdown_to_html print(markdown_to_html("# Welcome\n\nThis is **bold** and *italic* text.\n")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ```

Welcome

This is bold and italic text.

``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## `print()` vs. bare expressions Throughout this guide, examples use `print()` to display rendered output. This shows the string with newlines expanded, making the HTML structure easy to read. Without `print()`, Python displays the `repr()` of the string (with escaped `\n` characters and surrounding quotes), which is harder to scan visually. ::: The output is a complete HTML fragment with proper block-level structure. Headings become `

` through `

` elements, paragraphs are wrapped in `

` tags, and inline formatting maps to `` and ``. ## Working with Inline Formatting Markdown supports a rich set of inline constructs. Multimark handles all of them correctly, including nested formatting. ::: {#96caef26 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} text = """ This has **bold**, *italic*, `inline code`, and ***bold italic***. Here is a [link](https://example.com) and an ![image](logo.png "alt text"). """ print(markdown_to_html(text)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ```

This has bold, italic, inline code, and bold italic.

Here is a link and an .

``` ::: ::: Notice that the raw HTML output includes proper attribute encoding and escaping. Special characters like `<`, `>`, and `&` in your Markdown text are escaped automatically in the HTML output. ## Block-Level Elements Beyond paragraphs and headings, Markdown supports block quotes, code blocks, and lists. Each renders to its corresponding HTML structure. ::: {#a1da322f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fence = "```" blocks = ( "> A block quote with **emphasis**.\n\n" "- Item one\n" "- Item two\n" "- Item three\n\n" f"{fence}python\n" "def hello():\n" ' print("Hello!")\n' f"{fence}\n" ) print(markdown_to_html(blocks)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ```

A block quote with emphasis.

  • Item one
  • Item two
  • Item three
def hello():
    print("Hello!")
``` ::: ::: Fenced code blocks preserve their language annotation in a `class` attribute on the `` element, which is useful for client-side syntax highlighting libraries. ## Smart Punctuation Straight quotes and ASCII dashes look fine in source code but feel out of place in typeset prose. The `smart` option converts them to their typographic equivalents. ::: {#36cbe2f3 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} prose = '"It\'s a beautiful day," she said -- "let\'s go outside..."' print(markdown_to_html(prose, smart=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ```

“It’s a beautiful day,” she said – “let’s go outside…”

``` ::: ::: With `smart=True`, double quotes become curly quotes, single quotes become apostrophes, `--` becomes an en-dash, and `...` becomes an ellipsis character. This produces publication-quality output from plain ASCII input. ## Handling Raw HTML By default, multimark strips raw HTML from the input for security. This is the safe choice when processing untrusted content (user comments, forum posts, uploaded files). ::: {#d8bd87cb .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Raw HTML is stripped by default print(markdown_to_html("
Hello
")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ``` ::: ::: When you control the input and need HTML passthrough, set `unsafe=True`. ::: {#5b3fa3fd .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(markdown_to_html("
Hello
", unsafe=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ```
Hello
``` ::: ::: The `unsafe` flag affects both block-level HTML (like `
`) and inline HTML (like ``). It also allows potentially dangerous URL schemes like `javascript:` in links. Only enable this for content you fully trust. ## What Comes Next This page covered the basics of HTML rendering with multimark. The following pages explore GFM extensions, the other output formats, and the options system in depth. Each builds on what you have seen here, using the same straightforward API pattern: pass text in, get rendered output back.
